gloss: A woven or knitted cloth, especially one made in a factory.
examples: The town's economy ran on *textiles* for a hundred years.
She studies *textile* design at art school.
Cheap imported *textiles* put the old mill out of business.

gloss: The way the threads of a fabric are crossed over each other.
examples: This shirt has a tight *weave*, so the wind doesn't get through.
Hold it up to the light and you can see the *weave*.
Linen and cotton take very different *weaves*.

gloss: A fabric or garment made by looping yarn rather than weaving it.
examples: In the fall she lives in soft *knits* and jeans.
That sweater is a loose *knit*, so it stretches.
The store keeps the *knits* on the back wall.
contrast: The k is silent — *knit* sounds exactly like *nit*.

gloss: A smooth fabric that is shiny on one side and dull on the other.
examples: Her wedding dress was ivory *satin*.
The box was lined with black *satin*.
*Satin* slips off the hanger if you're not careful.
contrast: Not the Russian сатин — English *satin* is атлас; сатин is *sateen*.

gloss: A cotton fabric woven to give a soft sheen like satin.
examples: These sheets are cotton *sateen*.
*Sateen* feels cool against the skin.
She picked a *sateen* lining for the coat.
contrast: Stress on the second syllable, sa-TEEN, unlike *satin* (SAT-uhn).

gloss: A thick cotton fabric with raised ridges running down it.
examples: He wore brown *corduroy* pants to the interview.
*Corduroy* wears out at the knees first.
The jacket is lined *corduroy*, good for November.
contrast: False friend: Russian вельвет is English *corduroy*, while English *velvet* is бархат.

gloss: A rough woolen cloth woven from flecked yarn.
examples: My grandfather's *tweed* jacket still fits me.
The professor showed up in gray *tweed*.
*Tweed* is scratchy but it lasts forever.

gloss: A very light, sheer fabric of silk or synthetic thread.
examples: The sleeves were pale pink *chiffon*.
*Chiffon* snags on everything.
She threw a *chiffon* scarf over her shoulders.
contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable in American English: shih-FAHN.

gloss: A plain cotton cloth, often used for test garments or straining food.
examples: Strain the broth through a piece of *muslin*.
She sews the first version in cheap *muslin*.
The curtains are unbleached *muslin*.

gloss: A coarse brown cloth woven from jute, used for sacks and wrapping.
examples: The coffee came in *burlap* sacks.
We wrapped the tree roots in *burlap*.
She made table runners out of *burlap*.
contrast: Americans say *burlap*; the British call the same cloth hessian.

gloss: A cotton cloth woven in a small checked pattern, usually white and one color.
examples: The diner had red *gingham* on every table.
She wore a blue *gingham* dress.
*Gingham* always looks like summer to me.
contrast: The gh is not an h sound: say GING-uhm, never ging-HAM.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Cloth woven with crossing bands of color in a checked pattern.
examples: Every guy in the room had on a *plaid* shirt.
She bought two yards of green *plaid*.
The store was full of loud *plaids*.
contrast: Rhymes with *had*, not with *played*. And it is not Russian плед — a плед is a blanket or throw.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A Scottish checked pattern in which each clan has its own design.
examples: The band marched in full *tartan*.
Each family has its own *tartan*.
She collects scarves in old *tartans*.

gloss: A strong fabric woven so that diagonal lines show on the surface.
examples: The pants are cotton *twill*.
*Twill* holds a crease better than plain weave.
He ordered a jacket in navy *twill*.

ru: хаки (ткань и цвет); мн. ч. брюки цвета хаки
countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A dull yellowish-brown cotton cloth, or in the plural, pants made from it.
examples: The uniform was plain *khaki*.
He wore *khakis* and a blue blazer.
My *khakis* need to go to the cleaners.
contrast: Americans say KAK-ee; the British say KAH-kee. In the plural, *khakis* means the pants.

gloss: A weave whose short diagonal rows change direction, like the bones of a fish.
examples: He had on a gray *herringbone* coat.
The suit is *herringbone*, not solid.
*Herringbone* reads as a texture from across the room.

gloss: A checked pattern of broken, pointed shapes, usually black and white.
examples: She wore a *houndstooth* jacket.
*Houndstooth* never really goes out of style.
The chair was upholstered in *houndstooth*.

gloss: A light cotton cloth with puckered stripes that keep it off the skin.
examples: Every summer he pulls out the *seersucker* suit.
*Seersucker* doesn't need ironing, which is the point.
The dress was blue and white *seersucker*.

gloss: A smooth cotton fabric with fine ribs across it, common in dress shirts.
examples: The shirt is cotton *poplin*.
*Poplin* presses beautifully.
We ordered forty yards of white *poplin*.

gloss: A soft knitted fabric with a short thick pile, like a stretchy velvet.
examples: The tracksuit was maroon *velour*.
*Velour* seats were everywhere in seventies cars.
She bought a *velour* robe for the winter.

gloss: A fine net fabric used for veils, ballet skirts, and formal dresses.
examples: The skirt was layers of white *tulle*.
Her veil was a single piece of *tulle*.
*Tulle* catches on the slightest rough edge.
contrast: One syllable, and a homophone of *tool*.

gloss: A crisp shiny fabric that rustles when it moves.
examples: Her prom dress was green *taffeta*.
You could hear the *taffeta* from the hallway.
The lining is *taffeta*, so it slides on easily.

gloss: A thin, stiff, transparent fabric used for overlays and trim.
examples: The sleeves were sheer *organza*.
She wrapped the gift in *organza*.
*Organza* holds its shape better than chiffon.

gloss: A heavy fabric woven with a raised pattern, often in gold or silver thread.
examples: The chairs were covered in gold *brocade*.
She wore a jacket of stiff red *brocade*.
*Brocade* is too heavy for a summer dress.

gloss: A reversible fabric whose pattern is formed by the weave itself.
examples: The table was set with white *damask*.
*Damask* napkins come out for the holidays.
The curtains are heavy blue *damask*.

gloss: A cotton cloth printed with a small pattern, often in flowers.
examples: The quilt is pieced from old *calico*.
She sewed the girls matching *calico* dresses.
*Calico* was what everyone wore on the frontier.
contrast: In the US *calico* is printed cotton; in Britain it means plain unbleached cotton.

gloss: A tightly woven twill that sheds water, used for coats and suits.
examples: His raincoat was tan *gabardine*.
*Gabardine* holds a sharp crease.
The tailor recommended wool *gabardine* for the trousers.

gloss: A fabric with a lightly crinkled surface that drapes softly.
examples: The dress is black wool *crepe*.
*Crepe* hangs well and doesn't cling.
She lined the jacket with silk *crepe*.
contrast: Rhymes with *tape*, not with *creep*.

gloss: A closely woven cotton cloth with a crisp, matte finish, used for sheets.
examples: We switched to cotton *percale* sheets.
*Percale* feels cool the first night after washing.
The hotel uses white *percale* on every bed.

gloss: Wool yarn or cloth made from long fibers combed straight before spinning.
examples: The suit is fine *worsted* wool.
She knits mostly in *worsted*.
*Worsted* is smoother than ordinary woolen cloth.
contrast: Say WUUS-tid — the first syllable sounds like *wood*, not like *word*.

gloss: A silky wool from the angora goat, used in fluffy sweaters and coats.
examples: She wore a pale blue *mohair* sweater.
*Mohair* sheds on everything you own.
The blanket is *mohair* and wool.

gloss: A very soft fluffy wool that comes from angora rabbits.
examples: The cardigan is half *angora*.
*Angora* is warm but it pills quickly.
She spins her own *angora*.

gloss: A fine soft wool from merino sheep, worn next to the skin.
examples: These socks are *merino*, so they don't itch.
He hikes in a *merino* base layer.
*Merino* costs more but it's worth it.

gloss: Sheepskin tanned with the wool still on it, used for warm coats and boots.
examples: Her boots are lined with *shearling*.
He bought a *shearling* jacket for the winter.
*Shearling* is heavy but nothing is warmer.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: The skin of a sheep with the wool left on, or leather made from it.
examples: There was a *sheepskin* thrown over the chair.
The gloves are lined with *sheepskin*.
He sells *sheepskins* at the county fair.

gloss: The skin of an animal with the fur still attached.
examples: Trappers sold beaver *pelts* to the company.
A wolf *pelt* hung above the fireplace.
The *pelts* were stretched on wooden frames.

gloss: A soft fabric made from processed wood pulp rather than a natural fiber.
examples: The blouse is *rayon*, so wash it cold.
*Rayon* wrinkles the moment you sit down.
The label says sixty percent *rayon*.
contrast: Americans usually say *rayon* where Europeans say viscose — the same fiber.

gloss: A fiber made from dissolved cellulose, sold in the US mostly as rayon.
examples: The dress is *viscose* and it hangs beautifully.
*Viscose* loses its shape when it gets wet.
European labels list *viscose* instead of rayon.

gloss: A synthetic fiber that stretches far and springs back into shape.
examples: There's five percent *spandex* in these jeans.
The whole team wears *spandex*.
A little *spandex* keeps the knees from bagging out.
contrast: *Spandex* is the American word; elsewhere the same fiber is called elastane or Lycra.

gloss: A synthetic cloth of extremely fine threads that picks up dust and water.
examples: Wipe the screen with a *microfiber* cloth.
The couch is *microfiber*, so spills wipe right off.
*Microfiber* towels dry much faster than cotton.
contrast: Spelled *microfiber* in the US and microfibre in Britain.

gloss: A rough plant fiber spun into rope, sacks, and coarse cloth.
examples: The rug is woven from *jute*.
*Jute* twine is cheap and strong.
They shipped the grain in *jute* bags.

gloss: A tough plant fiber used for rope, canvas, and heavy cloth.
examples: Old ships were rigged with *hemp* rope.
The bag is woven *hemp*.
*Hemp* softens a lot after a few washes.

gloss: The blue-flowered plant whose stems are spun into linen thread.
examples: *Flax* has been grown here for centuries.
Linen is made from *flax*.
The field of *flax* turned pale blue in June.

gloss: A loose, thin cotton cloth used for straining and wrapping food.
examples: Line the strainer with *cheesecloth*.
Tie the herbs up in a square of *cheesecloth*.
*Cheesecloth* is in the aisle with the foil.

gloss: Cloth coated to make it waterproof, often used on kitchen tables.
examples: Grandma kept *oilcloth* on the kitchen table.
The picnic table was covered in checked *oilcloth*.
*Oilcloth* wipes clean with a sponge.

gloss: Open mesh material made of knotted or woven cord or thread.
examples: We put *netting* over the strawberries.
The hat had a bit of black *netting* on the brim.
*Netting* keeps the mosquitoes off at night.

gloss: A heavy cloth with a picture woven into it, hung on a wall.
examples: A faded *tapestry* covered the whole wall.
The museum keeps its *tapestries* out of direct light.
She's weaving a *tapestry* of the harbor.

gloss: A single thread or thin length of fiber twisted with others.
examples: Pull out a *strand* of the yarn and look at it.
The rope is made of three twisted *strands*.
A loose *strand* was hanging off the sleeve.

gloss: One of the strands twisted together to make a yarn or thread.
examples: This is a four-*ply* wool.
The pattern calls for a heavier *ply*.
Separate the *plies* and use just one.

gloss: A loose coil of yarn as it is sold in a store.
examples: I need three more *skeins* to finish the sweater.
She wound the *skein* into a ball.
The *skein* came undone in my bag.
contrast: Rhymes with *cane*, not with *seen*.

gloss: A small cylinder that thread or wire is wound onto.
examples: Pick up a *spool* of black thread while you're out.
The *spool* rolled under the couch.
She keeps her *spools* sorted by color.
contrast: Americans buy a *spool* of thread; the British buy a reel.

gloss: The small spool that holds the lower thread inside a sewing machine.
examples: The *bobbin* ran out halfway down the seam.
Wind a *bobbin* before you start.
She keeps spare *bobbins* in a tin.

gloss: A cylinder that thread, wire, or film is wound around.
examples: The mill ships the yarn on wooden *reels*.
He unwound a length off the *reel*.
Two empty *reels* were sitting by the loom.
contrast: Homophone of *real*. For sewing thread, Americans normally say *spool* instead.

gloss: Strong string made of two or more strands twisted together.
examples: Tie the box up with *twine*.
There's a ball of *twine* in the drawer.
The bundles were bound with *twine*.

gloss: A small metal cap worn on the finger to push a needle through cloth.
examples: Use a *thimble* or you'll stab yourself.
Her mother's silver *thimble* is in the sewing box.
He collects antique *thimbles*.

gloss: A small stuffed pad that pins and needles are stuck into.
examples: The *pincushion* is shaped like a tomato.
Stick the needle back in the *pincushion*.
She sews little *pincushions* out of scraps.

gloss: A pointed hand tool for punching holes in leather or heavy cloth.
examples: Punch the holes with an *awl* first.
The old *awl* had a worn wooden handle.
A saddler keeps several *awls* on the bench.
contrast: Sounds almost exactly like *all*; only the context tells them apart.

gloss: A machine that trims a seam and stitches over its raw edge at once.
examples: Finish the edges on the *serger*.
She saved up for a *serger*.
Most home sewers own a machine and a *serger*.
contrast: American *serger*; the British call the same machine an overlocker.

gloss: A frame or machine on which cloth is woven.
examples: The rug came off the *loom* yesterday.
There were two hundred *looms* on the factory floor.
She learned to warp a *loom* at sixteen.

gloss: The part of a loom that carries the crosswise thread back and forth.
examples: The *shuttle* flew across the loom.
He carved a new *shuttle* out of maple.
Old *shuttles* are smooth from years of use.

gloss: A rod that twists fiber into thread and holds the thread as it is spun.
examples: She twisted the wool onto the *spindle*.
A drop *spindle* is the simplest way to start spinning.
The mill had rows of humming *spindles*.

gloss: The lengthwise threads held on a loom while cloth is woven.
examples: The *warp* runs the length of the fabric.
It takes a whole day to set up the *warp*.
A broken *warp* thread stops the machine.

gloss: The crosswise threads woven over and under the warp.
examples: The *weft* is a darker blue than the warp.
She packs the *weft* down tight after each pass.
A loose *weft* makes a soft, open cloth.

gloss: The finished edge of woven cloth that does not fray.
examples: Line the pattern up with the *selvage*.
The *selvage* has the maker's name printed on it.
Cut the *selvages* off before you sew.
contrast: Usually spelled *selvage* in the US and selvedge in Britain.

gloss: The short raised fibers on the surface of velvet, suede, or corduroy.
examples: Cut all the pieces with the *nap* running the same way.
Brush the *nap* back up with a soft cloth.
Velvet looks darker against the *nap*.
contrast: Same spelling as *nap*, a short sleep — the fabric sense is uncountable.

gloss: The bottom edge of a skirt, dress, or coat, seen as a level.
examples: The *hemline* hit just below the knee.
*Hemlines* went up again that spring.
She let the *hemline* down two inches.

gloss: A tapered fold sewn into cloth so a garment fits the body's curves.
examples: Sew the *darts* before you join the side seams.
The *dart* pulls the waist in.
Two *darts* in the back will fix that gap.

gloss: A small piece of cloth sewn in to add room or strength.
examples: A *gusset* under the arm lets the sleeve move.
The bag has a wide *gusset* at the bottom.
Add *gussets* if the shirt feels tight across the back.

gloss: A shaped piece across the shoulders or hips that the rest of a garment hangs from.
examples: The shirt has a western *yoke* across the back.
Gather the skirt into the *yoke*.
Both *yokes* are cut on the bias.
contrast: A homophone of *yolk*, the yellow of an egg.

gloss: A piece of cloth sewn to an edge and turned inside to finish it neatly.
examples: Press the *facing* to the inside.
The neckline has a narrow *facing*.
Cut the *facings* from the same fabric.

gloss: Stiffening material placed between two layers of cloth to give shape.
examples: Iron the *interfacing* onto the collar.
Use light *interfacing* so the cuff still bends.
*Interfacing* is what keeps a waistband from folding over.

gloss: A soft layer of cotton or synthetic fiber used to fill a quilt or jacket.
examples: Lay the *batting* between the two layers.
Cotton *batting* shrinks a little the first wash.
She bought a whole roll of *batting*.
contrast: Same word as *batting* in baseball, but the quilting sense is uncountable.

gloss: Soft material put inside cloth to give bulk, warmth, or protection.
examples: The jacket has *padding* in the shoulders.
Pull the *padding* out and the coat is much lighter.
There's thin *padding* along the strap.

gloss: A narrow cord covered in fabric and sewn into a seam as trim.
examples: The cushions have white *piping*.
Red *piping* runs down the side of the trousers.
*Piping* makes a plain seam look finished.

gloss: A strip of cloth folded over a raw edge to cover and finish it.
examples: Stitch the *binding* around the edge of the quilt.
She used bias *binding* on the armholes.
The *binding* is a contrasting green.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Narrow woven trim sewn onto clothing, or a length of hair plaited together.
examples: The uniform had gold *braid* on the cuffs.
She wore her hair in two *braids*.
Sew the *braid* along the hem.
contrast: The decorative trim is uncountable — some *braid*; a plait of hair is countable — two *braids*.

gloss: Ribbon, lace, or braid added to a garment for decoration.
examples: The dress has lace *trim* at the collar.
Buttons and *trim* are down the next aisle.
A little velvet *trim* would dress it up.

gloss: A strip of gathered cloth sewn on as a decorative edge.
examples: The blouse has a *ruffle* down the front.
She hates *ruffles* on anything.
Add a narrow *ruffle* at the hem.

gloss: A narrow fold of cloth stitched down to shorten or decorate a garment.
examples: There are three little *tucks* on each side.
A *tuck* at the waist will take it in.
Press each *tuck* flat before you sew the next.

gloss: Stretchy cord or tape sewn into clothing so it pulls back into shape.
examples: The waistband has *elastic* in it.
Buy half an inch of *elastic* for the cuffs.
The *elastic* in these socks is shot.

gloss: A small reinforced hole in cloth for a lace or cord to pass through.
examples: Thread the cord through the *eyelets*.
One *eyelet* on the boot tore out.
The blouse is white cotton *eyelet*.

gloss: The opening in a garment that a sleeve is set into.
examples: The *armholes* are cut too high.
Measure around the *armhole* before you cut the sleeve.
Finish the *armhole* with bias tape.

ru: внутренний шов брючины (длина по внутренней стороне)
gloss: The seam running from the crotch to the bottom of a trouser leg, or its length.
examples: What's your *inseam*, thirty-two?
The tailor took an inch off the *inseam*.
Both *inseams* had come unstitched.
contrast: Americans ask for an *inseam*; the British ask for the inside leg.

gloss: The line around a garment or body at the narrowest part of the middle.
examples: The dress has a high *waistline*.
*Waistlines* dropped in the twenties.
Mark the *waistline* with chalk.
contrast: *Waist* sounds exactly like *waste*.

gloss: The measurement around a woman's chest, used in sizing clothes.
examples: Measure your *bust* under the arms.
The jacket is tight across the *bust*.
The chart lists *busts* from thirty-two to forty-four.

gloss: A tiny shiny disc sewn onto cloth for decoration.
examples: The top was covered in silver *sequins*.
A *sequin* came off and rolled under the table.
*Sequins* get everywhere once they start falling off.

gloss: A person's initials combined into one design and stitched onto cloth.
examples: His shirts have a small *monogram* on the pocket.
The towels came with our *monogram*.
She embroiders *monograms* on baby blankets.

gloss: Decorative patterns sewn onto cloth with colored thread.
examples: The jacket has gold *embroidery* on the back.
She does *embroidery* in the evenings.
That much *embroidery* takes weeks by hand.

gloss: Sewing and embroidery done by hand, especially as a craft.
examples: Her *needlework* hangs in the front hall.
*Needlework* was taught in every girls' school then.
He has no patience for *needlework*.
contrast: Uncountable — say a piece of *needlework*, never a needlework.

gloss: The craft of stitching layers of cloth and filling together.
examples: She took up *quilting* after she retired.
The *quilting* on this blanket is all done by hand.
There's a *quilting* class at the library.

gloss: Sewing that joins small pieces of different fabrics into one cloth.
examples: The quilt is *patchwork* in reds and blues.
She makes bags out of *patchwork*.
*Patchwork* uses up every last scrap.

gloss: The craft of making cloth by looping yarn with two long needles.
examples: She brought her *knitting* on the train.
*Knitting* keeps my hands busy.
He put the *knitting* down and answered the door.
contrast: The k is silent: NIT-ing.

gloss: The craft of making cloth by pulling loops of yarn through with a hook.
examples: The blanket is *crochet*, not knitting.
She learned *crochet* from her aunt.
There's a *crochet* border around the edge.
contrast: The final t is silent and ch is a sh sound: kroh-SHAY.

gloss: The making of cloth by crossing threads over and under each other.
examples: She teaches *weaving* at the craft school.
*Weaving* is slow work on a hand loom.
The museum has a room about *weaving*.

gloss: The work of joining or mending cloth with a needle and thread.
examples: There's a pile of *sewing* on the table.
I do all my *sewing* on Sunday afternoons.
She keeps her *sewing* things in a wicker basket.
contrast: *Sew* rhymes with *so*, not with *sue* — so it is SOH-ing, not SOO-ing.

gloss: A row or set of stitches, seen as the sewing on a finished item.
examples: The *stitching* on the pocket came loose.
You can see the *stitching* from the outside.
Contrast *stitching* is what makes jeans look like jeans.

gloss: Long loose stitches that hold cloth in place until it is sewn properly.
examples: Pull the *basting* out once the seam is done.
A little *basting* saves a lot of ripping later.
The *basting* is in white thread so it shows.

gloss: A knitting stitch made by pulling the yarn toward you, the opposite of a knit stitch.
examples: Knit one, *purl* two, all the way across.
The ribbing is knits and *purls*.
She can't tell a *purl* from a knit stitch yet.
contrast: A homophone of *pearl*, the jewel.

gloss: Clothes that need repair, or the work of repairing them.
examples: There's a basket of *mending* by the chair.
She did the *mending* while the radio played.
Nobody in this house does any *mending* anymore.

gloss: A paper shape used to cut out the pieces of a garment, or a design on cloth.
examples: Pin the *pattern* to the fabric before you cut.
She bought a *pattern* for a summer dress.
The two fabrics have very similar *patterns*.

gloss: A small sample piece of fabric shown to display color and texture.
examples: The store sent us three *swatches*.
Hold the *swatch* up next to the sofa.
Wash a *swatch* first to see if it shrinks.

gloss: The last short piece left on a bolt of cloth, usually sold cheap.
examples: She found a silk *remnant* for four dollars.
The *remnants* are in a bin by the register.
There's just enough in this *remnant* for a pillow.

gloss: A small leftover piece of cloth.
examples: Save the *scraps* for a quilt.
She wiped the machine with a *scrap* of flannel.
There's a bag of fabric *scraps* in the closet.

gloss: A large tightly packed bundle of cotton, wool, or hay bound for shipping.
examples: The wagon carried six *bales* of cotton.
A *bale* of raw wool weighs a couple hundred pounds.
*Bales* were stacked to the ceiling of the warehouse.

gloss: Someone who makes or alters clothes, especially suits and coats.
examples: Take the jacket to a *tailor*.
Her *tailor* has been on that corner for thirty years.
Good *tailors* are getting hard to find.

gloss: A woman whose job is sewing.
examples: His mother worked as a *seamstress*.
The *seamstress* pinned the hem in about a minute.
The factory employed forty *seamstresses*.

gloss: Someone who makes women's clothes to order.
examples: Her wedding dress was made by a local *dressmaker*.
The *dressmaker* wanted one more fitting.
There used to be *dressmakers* on every block.

gloss: Someone who makes or sells women's hats.
examples: The hats came from a *milliner* in Boston.
She trained as a *milliner* before the war.
Only a handful of *milliners* are left in the city.

gloss: Someone who repairs shoes.
examples: The *cobbler* put new heels on my boots.
There's a *cobbler* next to the dry cleaner.
*Cobblers* can fix almost anything but a broken sole.
contrast: In American English a *cobbler* is also a baked fruit dessert — peach *cobbler*.

gloss: Someone who makes cloth on a loom.
examples: The rugs are made by *weavers* in the mountains.
He's a *weaver* by trade.
The *weaver* showed us how the loom works.

gloss: Someone who prepares furs or makes and sells fur clothing.
examples: She left the coat with a *furrier* for the summer.
The *furrier* on Seventh Avenue closed last year.
*Furriers* used to store coats in cold vaults.

gloss: Someone who covers furniture in fabric and padding.
examples: The *upholsterer* redid the whole couch.
Ask an *upholsterer* how much fabric you'll need.
Good *upholsterers* charge by the yard.

gloss: A shop selling men's clothing and accessories.
examples: He bought the hat at an old *haberdashery* downtown.
The *haberdashery* had ties in every color.
Most of the city's *haberdasheries* are long gone.
contrast: In the US a *haberdashery* sells menswear; in Britain it sells sewing supplies.

gloss: A small shop selling fashionable clothes or accessories.
examples: She opened a *boutique* on Main Street.
The dress came from a *boutique* in the village.
Little *boutiques* line the whole block.

gloss: A factory where raw fiber is spun into yarn or woven into cloth.
examples: Half the town worked at the cotton *mill*.
The *mill* shut down in 1978.
The old *mills* along the river are apartments now.

gloss: A place where animal hides are turned into leather.
examples: The *tannery* was downwind of the town, for good reason.
He hauled hides to the *tannery* twice a week.
Most of the *tanneries* moved overseas.

gloss: The process of treating animal hides to turn them into leather.
examples: *Tanning* used to be done with tree bark.
The *tanning* gives the hide its color and smell.
Vegetable *tanning* takes months.

gloss: The cutting of wool off sheep.
examples: *Shearing* starts in late spring.
He hired three men for the *shearing*.
After the *shearing* the sheep look half their size.

gloss: The twisting of loose fiber into thread or yarn.
examples: *Spinning* was done at home before the mills came.
She does her own *spinning* and dyeing.
The *spinning* room was the loudest part of the factory.

gloss: The coloring of cloth or yarn by soaking it in dye.
examples: The *dyeing* is done before the cloth is cut.
Natural *dyeing* gives softer colors.
She teaches a workshop on indigo *dyeing*.
contrast: Keep the e: *dyeing* is coloring cloth, while *dying* means coming to an end of life.

gloss: A life-size model of a body used to display clothes or fit a garment.
examples: The coat looked better on the *mannequin*.
They redress the *mannequins* every Monday.
She pinned the muslin to a dress *mannequin*.
contrast: Three syllables, MAN-uh-kin — the qu is just a k sound.

gloss: A change made to a garment so that it fits better.
examples: The suit needs one small *alteration*.
*Alterations* are free if you buy the dress here.
The shop does *alterations* in two days.

gloss: An appointment at which clothes are tried on and adjusted.
examples: She has a *fitting* on Thursday.
It took three *fittings* to get the jacket right.
Bring the shoes you'll wear to the *fitting*.

gloss: Socks, stockings, and tights considered as goods for sale.
examples: *Hosiery* is on the second floor.
The store's *hosiery* department is tiny now.
She worked in *hosiery* for twenty years.
contrast: Uncountable — say a package of *hosiery*, never a hosiery.

gloss: Clothing made of knitted fabric, especially sweaters.
examples: The label is known for its *knitwear*.
*Knitwear* should be folded, not hung.
She designs *knitwear* for a company in Maine.
contrast: Uncountable — a piece of *knitwear*, never a knitwear.

gloss: Clothing made for sports or for casual everyday wear.
examples: *Sportswear* is at the back of the store.
The company started out in men's *sportswear*.
Half her closet is *sportswear*.
contrast: Uncountable — an item of *sportswear*, never a sportswear.

gloss: Clothing made to be worn for swimming.
examples: *Swimwear* goes on sale in August.
The store carries *swimwear* year-round.
Most *swimwear* has some spandex in it.
contrast: Uncountable — a piece of *swimwear*, never a swimwear.

gloss: Clothing made for men, taken as a category of goods.
examples: *Menswear* is on the third floor.
He's been designing *menswear* since college.
The show was all *menswear* this season.
contrast: Uncountable — say an item of *menswear*, never a menswear.

gloss: Women's underwear and nightclothes, especially the delicate kind.
examples: *Lingerie* is on the same floor as hosiery.
The shop sells silk *lingerie*.
She got *lingerie* as a shower gift.
contrast: The American pronunciation is lahn-zhuh-RAY, with the stress at the end.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The popular style of clothing at a given time, or a particular such style.
examples: She's worked in *fashion* her whole life.
Short jackets are back in *fashion*.
*Fashions* change faster than they used to.
contrast: The general sense is uncountable — in *fashion*; a specific trend is countable — the *fashions* of the fifties.

gloss: A particular design or cut of a garment.
examples: That *style* of collar suits him.
The jeans come in four *styles*.
It's an old *style*, but it's coming back.

gloss: A direction that fashion is moving in.
examples: Wide legs are the big *trend* this year.
She follows every *trend*.
Most *trends* last about two seasons.

gloss: The long raised platform models walk along in a fashion show.
examples: The coat looked enormous on the *runway*.
She's walked *runways* in Paris and Milan.
Nothing off that *runway* is going to end up in a store.
contrast: Americans say *runway*; the British say catwalk.

gloss: A narrow raised walkway, especially the one used in fashion shows.
examples: The models came down the *catwalk* one by one.
European magazines call it a *catwalk*.
There are *catwalks* above the stage for the lighting crew.

gloss: The set of clothes a designer shows for one season.
examples: Her fall *collection* was all gray and black.
The house shows two *collections* a year.
Nothing in the *collection* costs under a thousand dollars.

gloss: The overall outline a garment gives the body.
examples: The dress has a very straight *silhouette*.
*Silhouettes* got boxier in the eighties.
The coat softens the *silhouette*.
contrast: The h is silent: sil-oo-ET.

ru: драпировка, посадка ткани; мн. ч. портьеры
countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The way cloth hangs and falls, or in the plural, heavy curtains.
examples: Silk has a beautiful *drape*.
Close the *drapes* before you turn the light on.
The heavy *drapes* keep the room dark.
contrast: The hang of fabric is uncountable — good *drape*. In American homes *drapes* are what the British call curtains.

gloss: A set of clothes worn together as one look.
examples: She put together a whole *ensemble* for the wedding.
The hat completed the *ensemble*.
The exhibit shows a dozen *ensembles* from the period.
contrast: Pronounced the French way: ahn-SAHM-bul, with no n sound at the end.

gloss: The way a garment has been shaped and made.
examples: You can tell the quality by the *cut*.
It's a slim *cut* through the waist.
The two jackets are different *cuts* of the same cloth.

gloss: How well a garment sits on the body.
examples: The color is fine, but the *fit* is all wrong.
These come in a relaxed *fit* too.
The store carries three different *fits*.

gloss: One of the standard measurements clothes are made in.
examples: Do you have this in a bigger *size*?
The *sizes* run small in that brand.
She wears a *size* eight shoe.

gloss: A long band of color running across or down a fabric.
examples: The shirt has thin blue *stripes*.
Match the *stripes* at the side seam.
One white *stripe* runs down each leg.

gloss: A very narrow stripe in a pattern of many, typical of business suits.
examples: He wore a gray suit with faint *pinstripes*.
The *pinstripe* is chalk white.
*Pinstripes* make a jacket look more formal.

gloss: A pattern printed onto cloth rather than woven into it.
examples: She wore a floral *print*.
The *prints* this season are enormous.
A small *print* is easier to wear than a big one.

gloss: The soft shine on the surface of a fabric or fiber.
examples: Silk has a *luster* that polyester can't match.
The fabric loses its *luster* after a few washes.
Mercerized cotton has more *luster*.
contrast: Spelled *luster* in the US and lustre in Britain.

gloss: The craft of cutting and sewing fitted clothes, or the quality of that work.
examples: The *tailoring* on that coat is superb.
He learned *tailoring* from his father.
You pay for the fabric, but really you pay for the *tailoring*.

gloss: A factory where people sew clothes for low pay in bad conditions.
examples: The shirts were made in a *sweatshop*.
*Sweatshops* filled the lower floors of those buildings.
The article traced the jacket back to a *sweatshop* overseas.

gloss: Tiny loose fibers that collect on clothes or in a dryer.
examples: Clean the *lint* out of the dryer filter.
There's *lint* all over your black pants.
A roller takes the *lint* right off.
contrast: Uncountable — some *lint*, never a lint or lints.

gloss: Short soft loose fibers on the surface of cloth.
examples: The sweater is covered in *fuzz*.
Shave the *fuzz* off with a fabric razor.
New towels leave *fuzz* on everything.
contrast: Uncountable — say some *fuzz*, never a fuzz.

gloss: A pulled thread that sticks out of a knitted or woven fabric.
examples: There's a *snag* in my stocking.
Her ring left a *snag* in the sweater.
A few *snags* and the whole thing looks old.

gloss: A sharp line pressed into cloth, either on purpose or by accident.
examples: His trousers had a knife-sharp *crease*.
The shirt came out of the suitcase full of *creases*.
Iron the *crease* back in.

gloss: The amount a fabric gets smaller when it is washed.
examples: Allow for *shrinkage* when you cut the fabric.
There's about five percent *shrinkage* in cotton.
Prewashing takes care of most of the *shrinkage*.
contrast: Uncountable — some *shrinkage*, never a shrinkage.

gloss: A substance sprayed or soaked into cloth to make it stiff.
examples: He likes his collars with plenty of *starch*.
Spray a little *starch* before you press it.
The shirt was so full of *starch* it could stand up by itself.

gloss: A rope stretched outdoors for hanging washed clothes to dry.
examples: The sheets were flapping on the *clothesline*.
He strung a *clothesline* between two trees.
*Clotheslines* ran across every backyard on the street.
contrast: *Clothes* is said KLOHZ, exactly like *close* the verb — the th disappears.

gloss: A small clip for holding washing on a line.
examples: She had a *clothespin* in her mouth and a shirt in each hand.
The *clothespins* are in the bag on the porch.
One *clothespin* snapped in the cold.
contrast: American *clothespin*; the British say clothes peg.

gloss: The work of pressing wrinkles out of clothes with a hot iron.
examples: I have a whole basket of *ironing* to do.
He does the *ironing* on Sunday nights.
*Ironing* is the one chore she refuses.
contrast: *Iron* is said EYE-urn, not eye-RON, so this is EYE-ur-ning.
